transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I... I honestly wasn't sure if I should even make the appointment, because, you know, everyone gets stressed, especially in my line of work. I teach kindergarten, and, well, you can imagine the chaos. It’s a wonderful job, really it is, but it’s loud and there’s always something happening, always a little crisis to manage. But lately... well, honestly, what finally pushed me to come in is this physical thing that’s been happening. My shoulders and my neck, they just stay clenched all day long. It’s like I'm bracing for a classroom observation, you know? Like the principal is sitting right there in the corner with a clipboard, except she’s not, and the feeling just never ends. It just stays with me, from the moment I wake up, through circle time, through recess, all the way home. And then, by the evening, my jaw aches so badly from clenching it that I can hardly even enjoy playing my guitar, which is usually my way to unwind after dealing with five-year-olds all day. I just can't seem to get my body to let go of this... this tightness. It's exhausting, it really is.
Are you having any trouble sleeping at night?

Oh, sleep... sleep is just a complete disaster right now. I mean, you would think that after chasing five-year-olds around a classroom all day, managing meltdowns and tying shoes, I would just hit the pillow and completely pass out, right? That’s what people assume. But it is the exact opposite. 

Most nights, I just lie there in the dark for hours. The house is completely quiet, but my brain is just... it's like a television that someone left on at maximum volume and I can't find the remote. I'll spend hours, literally hours, just staring at the ceiling, replaying the most random or stressful things. I'll go over old interview answers from years ago, agonizing over whether I sounded foolish, or I'll start mentally tallying up our household bills, trying to calculate if the electric bill is going to be higher this month and how that affects the budget. And the paperwork—don't even get me started on the state licensing forms for the classroom. Those are a nightmare on their own. I'll lie there in bed panicking over whether I checked the right boxes on the safety compliance sheets or if the fire drill log was signed properly by the administration. It just loops and loops in my head.

And the worst part is, even when my body finally just gives out and I do manage to sleep, it doesn't last. I almost always wake up around four in the morning. And I don't just wake up peacefully, you know, slowly drifting awake. I wake up already completely tense—my neck and shoulders are already locked up again—and I am immediately calculating every single thing that could possibly go wrong that day. It's 4:00 AM, pitch black outside, and I'm lying there stressing about what happens if a parent gets upset about a scraped knee on the playground, or what if I lose control of the transition to art time. By the time my actual alarm goes off at six, I feel like I've already lived a full, stressful day. It's just... I'm so tired.
Are you experiencing any feelings of sadness or hopelessness?

Sadness? Um, no... no, I really wouldn't say that. I mean, I know sometimes people think that when you're this exhausted and run down, you must be, you know, depressed or down in the dumps, but it’s really not like that for me at all. It’s not a heavy, dark cloud kind of feeling. I definitely don't feel like giving up. 

I actually still really love my life, and I still absolutely love teaching. I've got my master's in early childhood education, I'm 53 years old, so I've been doing this for quite a while, and I still get a real kick out of the kids. Just yesterday, one of my boys, little Leo, finally figured out how to hold his safety scissors the right way without getting his thumb stuck, and I was just thrilled! So the joy is definitely still there. I'm not hopeless at all. 

It’s just... instead of feeling low or empty, I feel completely over-full, if that makes sense? Like a cup that's just overflowing with electricity. I'm honestly too wired, too keyed up to be sad. It’s a very high-energy kind of misery. If I ever feel like crying, it's strictly out of pure frustration because I just want my brain to stop spinning for five minutes so I can rest. But it's never because I feel hopeless about the future. I just feel... terrified of it, I guess? Or at least terrified of all the tiny, microscopic things that could potentially go wrong in the next twenty-four hours. So, no, not sad. Just running on a treadmill that's been set way, way too fast, and I can't seem to find the stop button.
Do you ever experience sudden episodes of intense fear or discomfort that reach a peak within minutes?

Sudden? Like, out of nowhere? Um... no. No, I... I really wouldn't say that. I know some people get that, right? Where they're just walking down the street or at the grocery store and suddenly they feel terrified out of the blue, and it hits them all at once like a wave. I had a co-teacher years ago who used to have to step out of the room into the hallway because that feeling would just hit her so fast and she couldn't catch her breath. But for me, it’s... it's really not like that at all. 

It's never a sudden spike that just lasts a few minutes and goes away. My thing is more like... well, it’s like a constant hum. You know those long fluorescent light tubes? I have one right above the reading nook in my classroom, and the ballast is going bad, so it just constantly buzzes. All day long. Just this low, steady, irritating vibration that you can never quite tune out. That’s exactly what this fear feels like. It doesn't suddenly flash and overwhelm me; it’s just already there, turned on, the second I wake up at four in the morning, and it just stays on. 

I never really have a baseline of feeling perfectly relaxed to suddenly spike *up* from, if you see what I mean. I’m just always up there, always bracing, always waiting for the other shoe to drop, whether I'm cutting out construction paper shapes for the kids or just trying to eat my dinner at home. It never peaks and then fades. So, no, not a sudden episode. Just this... endless, exhausting plateau of worry. Does that make sense? Because I definitely don't get those quick, intense episodes you're talking about, it's just always running in the background.
Are you finding it difficult to perform your daily tasks or responsibilities as a kindergarten teacher due to the way you've been feeling?

Well, it’s... it’s actually become a huge problem. I know I was just talking about little Leo and how much I love being around the kids, but the reality of my situation right now is that I'm only doing some very limited, piecemeal substituting and helping out. I’ve been trying so hard to get a permanent, full-time lead teacher position again for the upcoming term, but this constant worry is just completely derailing me. 

The process of just trying to secure a job has been a nightmare. I’ve actually missed several major application deadlines recently. I’ll sit down at my dining room table, open up the school district's portal on my laptop, and I just freeze. I start overthinking every single word on my resume, second-guessing my cover letter, worrying that I don't have the right certifications attached, and I'll just sit there paralyzed until the deadline literally passes. And then, on the rare occasions I actually do get all the paperwork in and they call me in, I’ve completely stumbled through the interviews. I had one two weeks ago, and they asked me a completely standard question about managing transition times, and my brain just flooded with every worst-case scenario. I ended up rambling, losing my train of thought, and I could just see the principal looking at me with this polite, confused smile. It was awful. 

And it's even affecting the small amount of work I *am* doing right now. Like, I used to love running the reading circles, but I’ve completely stopped volunteering for story-time. I just can't do it anymore—well, unless someone else handles all the planning. If another teacher picks out the books and sets up the activities, I can sit in the chair and read to the kids. But if I have to plan it myself? I will spend three days agonizing over whether the book is too long, if the kids will get restless and start acting out, or if I haven't tied it into the curriculum perfectly enough. It’s exhausting. 

So, honestly, this whole thing... it’s keeping me from getting back into the classroom in any reliable way. I have my master's degree, I have years of experience, I know how to teach! But right now, I can't even manage to get through a basic interview or plan a fifteen-minute story session without my brain turning it into a massive crisis.
Are you finding it difficult to maintain your relationships with friends and family due to the way you've been feeling?

Um... friends and family? Gosh, I... I really wouldn't say it's affecting them, no. I mean, my relationships are pretty much the same as they've always been. I know sometimes when people are struggling with things like this, they push people away or stop calling their friends, but I don't really do that. 

My sister, for example, she lives over in the next town, about a forty-minute drive depending on traffic—which, let me tell you, the traffic on I-95 has just been getting worse and worse lately, but anyway, we still talk on the phone every Sunday evening. We've done that for years. And I still see my friend Mark from my old teaching job. We try to grab coffee at least once a month at this little diner near my apartment. They have these amazing blueberry muffins, the kind with the crunchy sugar on top, you know? So, I still go out, I still talk to people. 

I mean, sure, maybe sometimes when I'm on the phone with my sister, my mind is racing a million miles an hour about whether I remembered to pay the electric bill or if I left the stove on—even though I haven't cooked anything on the stove in three days—but I still have the conversation. I still ask about her kids and listen to her talk about her garden. I don't think she even notices that I'm internally panicking half the time. And with Mark, I might be sitting there at the diner, staring at my muffin, worrying about an interview I have coming up, but I'm still physically there, right? I'm not canceling plans or hiding in my house. 

So, no, I wouldn't say it's difficult to maintain those relationships. I'm still very much involved in my family and my friendships. It's just... I'm bringing all this constant, exhausting worry along with me to every coffee date and phone call. But the relationships themselves? No, they're fine. I make sure of that. I just... I don't want to be a burden on anyone, so I just keep showing up and doing my best to act like everything is normal, even when my brain feels like it's going to explode.
Is your worry mostly about work and teaching, or does it also cover many other areas of your life?

Oh, it’s... it’s really everywhere. I mean, it certainly anchors itself around teaching because that's my life, that's what I do, but it doesn't stay there. It branches out like... well, like ivy, you know? It just creeps in and takes over everything else. It’s never just a simple, isolated thought of 'I hope I get a job.' 

My mind just keeps circling and circling in this endless, exhausting loop. I’ll be lying in bed, and first I'm agonizing over whether I'll ever get hired again, like we were just talking about with those applications and the frozen feeling. But then, almost immediately, that thought morphs into this intense panic about my past interactions. I'll start obsessing over whether I've somehow ruined my reputation with the parents in the district. You know how small these school communities can be—parents talk at the playground, they have their little group chats and email chains, and I'll convince myself that I said something slightly awkward during a drop-off two years ago, and now they all think I'm incompetent and I'm secretly blacklisted from every school in the county. 

And then, because I'm only doing that piecemeal substitute work, the financial panic sets in. I'm fifty-three now, so it’s not like I have decades and decades to bounce back and rebuild my savings. I'll start obsessively calculating my pension contributions in my head at two in the morning, worrying whether retirement is just completely slipping away from me. I'll picture myself at seventy, unable to pay my rent or afford groceries, all because I can't get my act together and secure a lead teacher spot right now. It just spirals into this massive dread about my entire future. 

But I think the worst part, the part that really breaks my heart, is how it attacks my actual ability to be around the kids. I'll think about a tiny, insignificant thing—like a small mistake I made during a story-time activity, maybe I stumbled over a word or I didn't transition them to the sensory table perfectly smoothly—and my brain will just run away with it. I'll actually start convincing myself that a mistake like that means I shouldn't be trusted with children anymore. That maybe I'm losing my touch, or I'm somehow a detriment to their early development. Which is ridiculous, right? I know it's ridiculous, I have a master's degree, I've been doing this for years! But the worry doesn't care about my degree. It just jumps from my career, to my reputation, to my financial survival, to my fundamental worth as an educator, over and over and over. 

So, to answer your question, no, it's definitely not just about the immediate tasks of teaching. It's... it's this massive web that just catches absolutely everything in my life. I don't know how to turn it off.
Do you feel like your constant worry is holding you back from enjoying or participating in activities outside of teaching that you normally would find pleasurable?

Oh, absolutely. It ruins them. It really does. Take my garden, for example. I have this little vegetable patch behind my place—I usually do heirloom tomatoes, some zucchini, a really nice trellis with runner beans. I used to love getting out there on a weekend. It was my sanctuary, you know? Just getting my hands in the dirt, completely away from the classroom and the district politics. 

But now... now I can barely enjoy it at all. I'll go out there with the best of intentions, thinking I'm just going to relax and have a nice, quiet hour to myself. But the second I'm out there, my mind just starts up. I try so hard to stop it, I really do. I try telling myself, you know, "Just make a mental list of what you need to do tomorrow and be done with it," or I'll try to just say a quick prayer to calm my nerves, or I'll tell myself, "Just weed this one section of the tomato bed, just focus on the next practical step right in front of you." I really try to force myself to just be present and pull the dandelions. 

But... it’s like my brain just won't let me. It doesn't matter what I do. One worry just hands off to another, like some kind of exhausting relay race. I'll start worrying about an interview, and then that instantly turns into worrying about my savings, and then that turns into worrying about whether I left a window open at the apartment. It just cascades. And before I know it, I'm just kneeling there in the dirt, completely frozen, and I've lost half the afternoon to it. 

I'll look at my watch and three hours have gone by, and I haven't actually enjoyed a single second of being outside. I haven't even finished weeding the one row! It's just so incredibly frustrating because I want to enjoy my life, I want to enjoy the things that used to bring me peace, but I just cannot control where my mind goes. It just hijacks my whole day, no matter how hard I try to distract myself with the things I'm supposed to love doing.
Are you experiencing any other physical symptoms, such as headaches or gastrointestinal issues, in addition to the muscle tension you've described?

Um, headaches or stomach things? You know, no, not really. I've actually never been much of a headache person, thankfully. My mother, she used to get these absolutely terrible migraines when I was growing up—the kind where she’d have to lie down in a completely dark room with a cold washcloth over her eyes for two days straight, and we all had to tiptoe around the house so we wouldn't disturb her. But I never inherited that from her, thank goodness. I mean, with the way my brain is constantly spinning and agonizing over every little detail of my life, you’d think I’d have a splitting headache all the time, but my head itself actually feels physically fine. It’s just the thoughts inside it that are the problem. 

And as for my stomach... no, my digestion is actually pretty normal. I’ve always been quite careful about what I eat. You know, when you work with preschoolers or kindergarteners, you can't exactly be running off to the restroom in the middle of a messy finger-painting activity or when you're trying to corral fifteen kids for circle time. You have to be present, you have to be the anchor in the room. So I've always stuck to a really predictable, plain diet—just oatmeal with a few sliced bananas in the morning, maybe a simple turkey sandwich on whole wheat for lunch. Nothing too spicy or rich. So my stomach handles everything just fine. Sometimes I might forget to eat lunch entirely because I'm so wrapped up in worrying about my savings or analyzing an interaction I had with the principal three weeks ago, but when I do finally sit down to eat, it doesn't upset my stomach at all. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I have any gastrointestinal issues or headaches. It really just comes back to that muscle tension you brought up. That’s where it all lives physically for me. It’s like my shoulders are practically glued to my earlobes by the end of the day, and my jaw is just clamped shut from bracing myself against my own thoughts, but... yeah, no stomach aches or head pain. Just the tension and the endless, exhausting worrying.
Are there any areas of your life outside of teaching where you feel like your worry is causing you significant distress or impairment?

Well, outside of the actual act of teaching itself... yes, absolutely, because it's completely paralyzed my ability to manage my daily life and, ironically, to get back to teaching. I mean, just the sheer logistics of my life are falling apart right now. 

Take the job hunt, for instance. I'll sit down at my computer—I have this little oak desk in the corner of my living room that I try to keep organized specifically for this purpose—and I'll open up the district portal to look at the openings. And instead of just filling out the forms like a capable adult, I just stare at the screen. I get so overwhelmed by the 'what ifs' and the dread that I've actually missed application deadlines. Several of them, actually. Good positions, too, but I just let the clock run out on the deadline because I was too paralyzed by the worry to just hit submit. 

And then, on the rare occasions when I do force myself to follow through and I actually get a call back, I've just completely stumbled through interviews. I had one a few weeks ago at a really lovely little magnet school, and the principal asked me a basic question about lesson planning—something I could literally answer in my sleep! But my mind was just racing, worrying about what they were thinking, whether they could tell I was anxious, if they thought I was too old for the role... and I just babbled. I stumbled over my words so badly. I could see them looking at me, and I just knew I was ruining it in real-time, but I couldn't stop.

It’s even bleeding into my community stuff, things that used to just be purely for fun. I used to love doing the weekend story-time at the public library. It was wonderful, just me and the kids and a big stack of picture books. But lately... I've stopped volunteering for story-time entirely, unless someone else handles all the planning. I just can't bear the weight of organizing it myself anymore, the fear of messing it up or choosing the wrong book or losing the kids' attention is just too heavy. I told the head librarian I can only be a backup reader now. 

So, really, this whole thing... the anxiety is just keeping me from getting back into the classroom in any reliable way. It’s dictating everything I do, or rather, everything I can't do anymore. It's just so frustrating to watch yourself fail at basic steps and not be able to stop it.
Is there a particular theme or topic that your worries most often center around?

Well, it's funny you ask if there's a particular theme, because honestly, it feels like it's just a giant web of everything, but I suppose if I really step back and look at it, it all centers around my career, my standing, and just... my entire future. 

I'll just sit in my armchair for hours, staring out the window, and my mind just keeps circling and circling about whether I'll ever get hired again. I mean, I'm fifty-three years old with a master's degree. I'm not exactly a twenty-two-year-old fresh out of college who they can pay the absolute base salary. I constantly worry that districts are looking at my resume and just seeing a liability, or someone who costs too much, and I just obsess over the idea that my days in the classroom are permanently over. 

And then, of course, that instantly spirals into this massive panic about my reputation. I have spent decades building trust in this community. Decades. But lately, I am constantly agonizing over whether I've completely ruined my reputation with the parents. You know how parents are these days—they talk, they have these neighborhood Facebook groups and group texts, and I just convince myself that they're all whispering about me. I worry they think I've lost my touch, or that I'm unreliable now because I'm not teaching full-time. I'll analyze a five-minute conversation I had with a former student's mother at the grocery store for three weeks, completely terrified that I said something wrong.

Which, naturally, leads right into the financial terror of it all. Because if I can't get hired, and my reputation is ruined, then I start doing the math in my head, just obsessively worrying about whether my retirement is slipping away. I had a very specific plan, you know? A timeline for my state pension and my savings, and now I feel like I'm just watching it all evaporate right in front of my eyes because I can't get myself together to secure a new position. 

But I think the most exhausting part, the part that really shows how ridiculous my brain is being, is how I agonize over the absolute tiniest things. Like I mentioned that library story-time earlier? I'll make one tiny, insignificant mistake—maybe I accidentally skip a page in a picture book, or I stumble over the words in a little finger-play song—and my brain will just latch onto it like a vice. I will spend days completely convinced that this one small mistake in a volunteer story-time activity means I am fundamentally incompetent and shouldn't even be trusted with children anymore. It's like my mind takes this massive, illogical leap from a skipped page to "you are a fraud and a danger to the profession." It just keeps circling these exact same fears, over and over, and I can't seem to find the off switch.
Are you finding it difficult to connect with others or maintain social relationships due to your constant worrying?

Social relationships... you know, connecting with people? I... actually, I wouldn't say that's an issue for me, surprisingly enough. I mean, you'd think it would be, with how much space this worry takes up in my head, but no, I still have my friends. I've always been a very social person, very community-oriented—which I suppose comes with the territory when you've been in early childhood education as long as I have. You have to be able to talk to anyone, from a crying four-year-old to a very demanding PTA president. 

So, my core group of friends... we're actually mostly former and current teachers. We've known each other for, oh, gosh, it has to be going on twenty-five years now. We still meet up. We have this standing breakfast thing every other Saturday morning at this little diner downtown—the one over on Elm Street, with the green awnings, I don't know if you know it, but they make the most incredible blueberry pancakes. Anyway, we still go. I never cancel on them. I make a point of showing up, because I know if I just stay in my house all weekend, I'll just stew in my own thoughts. 

Now, do I talk their ears off about my job hunt and my retirement fears while we're sitting there trying to enjoy our coffee? Yes, absolutely. I probably sound like a broken record to them at this point, just going over and over the same anxieties about whether my resume is too old or if I'm going to have to dip into my savings. But they are wonderful, patient people, and they just listen and nod and pour me more decaf. 

And I still talk to my sister on the phone every Sunday evening, like clockwork. She lives two states over, but we never miss a call. I might spend half the conversation agonizing over that grocery store interaction I mentioned earlier, completely overanalyzing what I said to that parent, but the connection itself is still there. I haven't pulled away from anyone or stopped returning calls. If anything, I probably lean on people a bit too much right now, just needing a sounding board for all this... this noise in my head. But no, I haven't lost any friends over this, and I don't find it hard to connect. I just... I bring the worry with me when I socialize, I suppose.
Are there any daily activities outside of teaching that you used to enjoy but can no longer do because of your worrying?

Activities... well, yes. It's actually the main reason I finally made the appointment to see you. I've always been a big music person. I have this gorgeous old acoustic guitar—it's a Martin, I actually bought it way back when I was finishing up my master's degree—and playing it has always been my evening ritual. Just sitting on the porch or in the living room, picking out some folk tunes, a little James Taylor, that sort of thing. It used to be the absolute perfect way to unwind after a loud day with a room full of four- and five-year-olds. 

But lately... I just can't do it. And it's not just because my mind is racing, though obviously it is, but honestly, what finally pushed me to come in is what this worry is doing to me physically. My shoulders and my neck... they just stay completely, rigidly clenched all day long. It's this intense tightness, right up through the base of my skull. It feels exactly like that physical response you get when you're bracing for a formal classroom observation from the superintendent—you know that stiff, panicked, hold-your-breath posture?—except it never ends. I walk around like that from the moment I wake up, just waiting for the other shoe to drop. 

And because of that, by the time evening rolls around and I try to just sit down and play my guitar, my jaw aches so badly from clenching my teeth all day, and my shoulders are so locked up, that I can hardly even hold the instrument comfortably, let alone actually enjoy playing it. I just sit there with my hands on the strings, completely tight and aching, and I end up just putting it back in the case. It's heartbreaking, really, to lose that release just because my body is wound up like a coiled spring all the time.
Are there any places or situations that you actively avoid because of your worrying?

Avoid? Um... no, actually. No, I don't think I do. I mean, you would think I would, wouldn't you? With all this constant dread just hanging over me all day, every day, you'd think I'd just want to lock the front door, pull the blinds shut, and hide from the world. But I really don't do that. I still go everywhere I normally would. 

I still go to the grocery store, for instance. Even though, like I was saying earlier, I might spend three entire weeks agonizing over a five-minute chat I had by the produce section with a former student's mother, I still push my cart right down those aisles the very next week. And I still go to the public library for that volunteer story-time, every single Tuesday at 10 AM, completely without fail. I'll sit there in the little reading circle, you know, on those tiny primary-colored alphabet carpets, surrounded by toddlers, absolutely terrified that I'm going to mispronounce a word or skip a page in a picture book and somehow prove that I'm unfit to ever teach again... but I still show up and do it. I don't avoid it. 

I think, honestly, if I started avoiding places because of the worry, I'd just have to avoid absolutely everywhere, because the worry isn't really... it isn't *in* the grocery store, and it isn't *in* the library, or the diner with my friends. It's just right here in my head. So no matter where I drive my car, no matter what situation I walk into, the worry is just riding shotgun anyway. It never stays home. So, no, I haven't started avoiding any specific places or anything like that. I just sort of... take it all with me and suffer through it, I suppose.
Are you finding it difficult to maintain intimacy or a sense of connection with your loved ones due to your constant worrying?

Intimacy... well, I suppose that goes back to what I was saying earlier about my friends and my sister. I don't think I'm losing that connection, no. I mean, my wife, Sarah—we've been married for nearly thirty years now, since right after I started teaching, actually. And she's... she's just a saint, really. She sees how wound up I am, how I'm just pacing the house at night, worrying about our retirement accounts and whether I'm going to get hired anywhere else. 

And she doesn't pull away. If anything, she tries to pull me closer. She'll sit with me on the couch while I'm just obsessing over some minor detail of my resume, and she'll just hold my hand. My hands are usually freezing cold these days, just from the stress of it all, I think, but she just holds them. So the connection is there. The intimacy is there. 

But... I will say, I feel incredibly guilty about it. Because I know I'm not fully present. When we're sitting there, watching a movie or having dinner, she's trying to talk to me about her day—she works in administration over at the community college, so she always has these long stories about the faculty meetings—and I'm nodding, and I'm looking right at her, but half my brain is just spinning out of control. I'm thinking, "Did I update the references on that application? What if my former principal doesn't give me a good recommendation? What if we have to downsize the house?" 

So, I'm there with her, physically, and I love her just as much as I ever did, maybe more, because she's putting up with all of this. But I know I'm distracted. I know I'm not giving her the best version of myself right now. I'm just... I'm so consumed by the noise in my own head that I'm sure it must feel to her like I'm a million miles away sometimes, even when I'm sitting right next to her. But no, the relationship itself hasn't broken down. I just... I wish I could turn it off for her sake, you know? Just for one evening, just to be completely, one hundred percent there with her.
Are you finding it difficult to connect with others or form new relationships because of your constant worrying?

New relationships? Connect with others? Well, I suppose... no, not really. I mean, I don't think I'm having any more trouble than usual, to be perfectly honest. I'm fifty-three years old, you know? At this stage in life, especially when you've been a kindergarten teacher for as long as I have, your social circle is pretty well established. I've got Sarah, obviously, and my sister, and a handful of friends I've known since my master's program. We still go to the diner on Thursday nights—well, most Thursday nights, anyway, unless one of us is grading assessments or something. 

So it's not like I'm out there trying to join new clubs or, I don't know, strike up deep, meaningful friendships with strangers at the coffee shop. That's just not really where my life is right now, worry or no worry. I mean, sure, if I *were* trying to meet new people, I'm sure the worrying would make it an absolute nightmare. I can just imagine sitting across from someone new, my mind racing a mile a minute, agonizing over whether I'm talking too much about my job situation or if I have something in my teeth or if they think I'm a complete wreck... but since I'm not actually putting myself in those situations, I can't really say it's stopping me. 

I interact with the parents at school, of course, and the other teachers, and I think I do fine with that. I mean, I might spend three weeks overthinking a five-minute conversation by the cubbies, like I mentioned earlier, but in the moment, I'm still smiling, still shaking hands, still making the connection, you know? They probably have no idea that underneath it all, my stomach is in knots and my shoulders are up around my ears. So, no, I wouldn't say the worry is preventing me from forming connections. It just... it makes the connections I do have feel exhausting sometimes, but it doesn't stop me from making them, if that makes sense.
Are you finding it difficult to connect with others or maintain social relationships due to your constant worrying?

I feel like we might be circling the same drain here a little bit, Doctor, because like I was just saying... no, not really. Maintaining them isn't the issue. Take my friends from my master's program, for example. The ones I meet at the diner? We've been doing that since, gosh, 1996? Maybe 1997? Right around the time Sarah and I got married and I first started teaching kindergarten. And I haven't stopped going. I mean, I haven't missed a Thursday unless I was physically ill or stuck at a late parent-teacher conference. So I am maintaining those relationships. I'm still showing up. 

Now, sure, I might sit there in the booth, picking at my fries, completely zoned out because I'm terrified about my pension or whether the school board is going to cut early childhood funding again. I'll just sit in my armchair for hours, staring out the window, and my mind just keeps circling and circling about whether I'll ever get hired again. I mean, I'm fifty-three years old with a master's degree. I'm not exactly a twenty-two-year-old fresh out of college who they can pay the absolute base salary. I constantly worry that districts are looking at my resume and just seeing a liability, or someone who costs too much, and I just obsess over the idea that my days in the classroom are permanently over. 

And then, of course, that instantly spirals into this massive panic about my reputation. I have spent decades building trust in this community. Decades. But lately, I am constantly agonizing over whether I've completely ruined my reputation with the parents. You know how parents are these days—they talk, they have these neighborhood Facebook groups and group texts, and I just convince myself that they're all whispering about me. I worry they think I've lost my touch, or that I'm unreliable now because I'm not teaching full-time. I'll analyze a five-minute conversation I had with a former student's mother at the grocery store for three weeks, completely terrified that I said something wrong.

Which, naturally, leads right into the financial terror of it all. Because if I can't get hired, and my reputation is ruined, then I start doing the math in my head, just obsessively worrying about whether my retirement is slipping away. I had a very specific plan, you know? A timeline for my state pension and my savings, and now I feel like I'm just watching it all evaporate right in front of my eyes because I can't get myself together to secure a new position. 

But I think the most exhausting part, the part that really shows how ridiculous my brain is being, is how I agonize over the absolute tiniest things. Like I mentioned that library story-time earlier? I'll make one tiny, insignificant mistake—maybe I accidentally skip a page in a picture book, or I stumble over the words in a little finger-play song—and my brain will just latch onto it like a vice. I will spend days completely convinced that this one small mistake in a volunteer story-time activity means I am fundamentally incompetent and shouldn't even be trusted with children anymore. It's like my mind takes this massive, illogical leap from a skipped page to "you are a fraud and a danger to the profession." It just keeps circling these exact same fears, over and over, and I can't seem to find the off switch.

Social relationships... you know, connecting with people? I... actually, I wouldn't say that's an issue for me, surprisingly enough. I mean, you'd think it would be, with how much space this worry takes up in my head, but no, I still have my friends. I've always been a very social person, very community-oriented—which I suppose comes with the territory when you've been in early childhood education as long as I have. You have to be able to talk to anyone, from a crying four-year-old to a very demanding PTA president. 

So, my core group of friends... we're actually mostly former and current teachers. We've known each other for, oh, gosh, it has to be going on twenty-five years now. We still meet up. We have this standing breakfast thing every other Saturday morning at this little diner downtown—the one over on Elm Street, with the green awnings, I don't know if you know it, but they make the most incredible blueberry pancakes. Anyway, we still go. I never cancel on them. I make a point of showing up, because I know if I just stay in my house all weekend, I'll just stew in my own thoughts. 

Now, do I talk their ears off about my job hunt and my retirement fears while we're sitting there trying to enjoy our coffee? Yes, absolutely. I probably sound like a broken record to them at this point, just going over and over the same anxieties about whether my resume is too old or if I'm going to have to dip into my savings. But they are wonderful, patient people, and they just listen and nod and pour me more decaf. 

And I still talk to my sister on the phone every Sunday evening, like clockwork. She lives two states over, but we never miss a call. I might spend half the conversation agonizing over that grocery store interaction I mentioned earlier, completely overanalyzing what I said to that parent, but the connection itself is still there. I haven't pulled away from anyone or stopped returning calls. If anything, I probably lean on people a bit too much right now, just needing a sounding board for all this... this noise in my head. But no, I haven't lost any friends over this, and I don't find it hard to connect. I just... I bring the worry with me when I socialize, I suppose.

Activities... well, yes. It's actually the main reason I finally made the appointment to see you. I've always been a big music person. I have this gorgeous old acoustic guitar—it's a Martin, I actually bought it way back when I was finishing up my master's degree—and playing it has always been my evening ritual. Just sitting on the porch or in the living room, picking out some folk tunes, a little James Taylor, that sort of thing. It used to be the absolute perfect way to unwind after a loud day with a room full of four- and five-year-olds. 

But lately... I just can't do it. And it's not just because my mind is racing, though obviously it is, but honestly, what finally pushed me to come in is what this worry is doing to me physically. My shoulders and my neck... they just stay completely, rigidly clenched all day long. It's this intense tightness, right up through the base of my skull. It feels exactly like that physical response you get when you're bracing for a formal classroom observation from the superintendent—you know that stiff, panicked, hold-your-breath posture?—except it never ends. I walk around like that from the moment I wake up, just waiting for the other shoe to drop. 

And because of that, by the time evening rolls around and I try to just sit down and play my guitar, my jaw aches so badly from clenching my teeth all day, and my shoulders are so locked up, that I can hardly even hold the instrument comfortably, let alone actually enjoy playing it. I just sit there with my hands on the strings, completely tight and aching, and I end up just putting it back in the case. It's heartbreaking, really, to lose that release just because my body is wound up like a coiled spring all the time.

I'll sit there in the little reading circle, you know, on those tiny primary-colored alphabet carpets, surrounded by toddlers, absolutely terrified that I'm going to mispronounce a word or skip a page in a picture book and somehow prove that I'm unfit to ever teach again... but I still show up and do it. I don't avoid it. 

I think, honestly, if I started avoiding places because of the worry, I'd just have to avoid absolutely everywhere, because the worry isn't really... it isn't *in* the grocery store, and it isn't *in* the library, or the diner with my friends. It's just right here in my head. So no matter where I drive my car, no matter what situation I walk into, the worry is just riding shotgun anyway. It never stays home. So, no, I haven't started avoiding any specific places or anything like that. I just sort of... take it all with me and suffer through it, I suppose.

So, I'm there with her, physically, and I love her just as much as I ever did, maybe more, because she's putting up with all of this. But I know I'm distracted. I know I'm not giving her the best version of myself right now. I'm just... I'm so consumed by the noise in my own head that I'm sure it must feel to her like I'm a million miles away sometimes, even when I'm sitting right next to her.
